title: Musculoskeletal injury in the masters runners
authors: McKean KA, Manson NA, Stanish WD
population: 2,886 runners in the Hood to Coast relay (34% masters, aged 40 or over), retrospective one-year injury survey
findings: Overall injury rate was 46%; significantly more masters runners were injured than younger runners (P < 0.05), and more masters suffered multiple injuries (P < 0.001).
Significantly more masters were male, had 7+ years of running experience, ran more than 30 miles per week and 6 or more times per week, and wore orthotics (P < 0.001).
Soft-tissue injuries to the calf, Achilles and hamstrings were more prevalent in masters (P < 0.001); younger runners had more knee and leg injuries (P < 0.005).
Running more times per week increased the risk of injury for both groups; the authors say differences may reflect differences in training intensity.
limitations: Retrospective self-report (recall bias), cross-sectional, relay-event sample; masters trained more (experience, weekly miles, sessions per week), so age is confounded with exposure.
implications: For runners 40 or over, give extra attention to calf, Achilles and hamstring loading: calf and posterior-chain strength and gradual progression of hills and speedwork.

Do not push frequency: a soft default cap on run days per week (for example 6) with a rest or cross-training day is a design suggestion derived from the finding that frequency raised risk; the paper gives no threshold.
Treat increased injury susceptibility as modest and exposure-related; use conservative weekly load progression rather than an age-specific rule.

verification.notes: Crossref and Europe PMC abstract match. Added the abstract's confounder data (6+ times/week, >30 mi/wk) supporting the exposure confound.
